name: Luro
confidence_why: The only statement on Luro stress is an incidental remark in Abbi and Vysakh's 2020 word-formation article, where three disyllabic verbs carry second-syllable stress that moves to the first syllable under infixation unless the second syllable is closed; their 2020 dictionary marks no stress, no phonological description of the language has been published, and Sidwell 1889 and Man 1889 describe other Nicobarese languages, so no stress rule for Luro can be stated with confidence.
catalog_citation: Abbi, Anvita & Vysakh R. 2020. Aspects of word formation processes in Luro: The endangered language of the Nicobar Islands. Asian Languages and Linguistics 1(1): 9-33. doi:10.1075/alal.00001.abb (open access)
catalog_quote: Another nominalizing affix that shows productivity is the infix /<ən>/ which is inserted after the first syllable of the base word. It derives nouns from verbs. If the first syllable of the base word ends with a vowel the first vowel of the infix ə is dropped. However, if the vowel of the first syllable is ə then it is raised and fronted to i because the addition of the infix shifts the stress from the second syllable to the first syllable. Interestingly, the stress does not shift if the second syllable is a closed syllable like in case of (37). Subsequently, according to the rule the reduced vowel of the infix ə is dropped to maintain the CVCVC structure. Consider Examples (35), (36) and (37). (33) t̪ikəːk ‘sing’ → t̪i<n>kəːk ‘song’ (34) kihɔk̚ ‘breathe’ → ki<n>hɔk̚ ‘breath’ (35) kəˈt̪ɔkə ‘dance’ → ˈki<n>t̪ɔkə ‘dance’ (36) kəˈwokə ‘to point’ → ˈki<n>wokə ‘index finger’ (37) həˈpip ‘to whistle → hə<nˈ>pip ‘whistle’
world_status: statement found in an open source

At sec. 3.2.1.2, journal pp.16-17 (pp.8-9) the passage is present as quoted: 'Another nominalizing affix that shows productivity is the infix /<ən>/ which is inserted after the first syllable of the base word.. because the addition of the infix shifts the stress from the second syllable to the first syllable. Interestingly, the stress does not shift if the second syllable is a closed syllable like in case of (37).' followed (after (33)-(34), covered on verification's [..]) by '(35) kəˈt̪ɔkə 'dance' → ˈki<n>t̪ɔkə 'dance' (36) kəˈwokə 'to point' → ˈki<n>wokə 'index finger' (37) həˈpip…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general rule is stated. What the passage shows: underived verbs with an initial ə-syllable carry stress on the second syllable (kəˈt̪ɔkə, həˈpip, i.e. iambic over the first two syllables, final -ə unstressed); when the -n- infix closes the first syllable (and its ə becomes i) stress moves to that first, now closed, syllable (ˈkin.t̪ɔ.kə), except that a closed second syllable keeps the stress (hən.ˈpip). This is consistent with a weight-sensitive, schwa-avoiding stress within a broadly iambic Nicobaric root template, but the authors do not formulate it; treat as partial first-hand evidence pending the 2023 sketch.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress does not shift to the infixed first syllable when the second syllable is closed (ex. 37 həˈpip → hənˈpip).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms (isolated lexical items in a morphology paper); stress marks appear only on examples (35)-(37); elsewhere in the article forms are unmarked for stress. Article is morphology-focused; phonology overview (sec. 2, pp. 12-13) has inventories and CVCV syllable template but no prosody paragraph.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Luro/Lurö as spoken on Teressa Island (= Glottolog tere1272, ISO tef); Abbi & Vysakh's fieldwork 2018-20 on Teressa. The Bompoka variety (Pauhut/Poatat) is not separately treated. Man 1889's stress rules held by the project are for Central Nicobarese (Nancowry, not tere1272) and Sidwell 2018's iambic-root statement is pan-Nicobaric/comparative; neither was used as the statement.

sources.note: Sec.2 (pp.12-13) gives vowel/consonant inventories and CVCV syllable preference but no stress section. The only stress statement is incidental, in sec.3.2.1.2 (p.16-17) on the nominalizing infix -ən-: base verbs are transcribed with stress on the second syllable (kəˈt̪ɔkə, kəˈwokə, həˈpip); infixation 'shifts the stress from the second syllable to the first syllable' (ˈkint̪ɔkə, ˈkinwokə) 'but the stress does not shift if the second syllable is a closed syllable' (hənˈpip). No general word-stress rule stated.
